bodyText:
What is an Input Device?

An input device is a hardware component that allows a user to enter data, instructions, or commands into a computer system. The computer processes this input and produces a result through an output device. Input devices convert human-readable data into a binary form that the computer can understand.

Keyboard

The keyboard is the most common input device. It is used to type text, numbers, and commands. The standard layout is called QWERTY, named after the first six letters on the top row of letter keys.

The keyboard is divided into several groups of keys:

  • Alphanumeric keys: letters, numbers, and punctuation marks.
  • Function keys: F1 to F12, placed along the top row, used for shortcuts and special commands in different programs.
  • Numeric keypad: a calculator-style set of number keys on the right side of a standard keyboard.
  • Navigation keys: arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up, and Page Down, used to move the cursor.
  • Control keys: Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Enter, Backspace, Delete, and Esc, used alone or in combination with other keys.

The QWERTY layout was developed for the typewriter by Christopher Latham Sholes. It was designed to prevent the mechanical type bars of early typewriters from jamming.

Mouse

The mouse is a pointing device used to move the cursor on the screen, select objects, and open programs. The user moves the mouse on a flat surface, and the pointer on the screen moves in the same direction.

Common mouse actions are click, double-click, right-click, drag and drop, and scroll. Modern mice are usually optical or laser mice, which use light instead of a rolling ball to detect movement. A wireless mouse connects to the computer through radio signals or Bluetooth instead of a cable.

The computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart. He demonstrated it publicly in 1968 in a presentation now known as the Mother of All Demos.

Scanner

A scanner is an input device that copies a physical document, photograph, or image into digital form so that it can be stored, edited, or displayed on a computer.

Common types of scanners are flatbed scanners, in which the document is placed face down on a glass plate; sheet-fed scanners, which pull pages through automatically; and handheld scanners, which are moved over the document by hand. Scanner quality is measured in DPI, or dots per inch: a higher DPI means a sharper and more detailed image.

Scanned text can be converted into editable text by OCR software. OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition. Related recognition technologies are OMR, Optical Mark Recognition, used for checking marked answer sheets, and MICR, Magnetic Ink Character Recognition, used for reading codes printed on bank cheques.

Other Common Input Devices

Other input devices include the microphone, which inputs sound; the joystick, used mainly for games; the touch screen, which accepts input by touch; the webcam, which inputs video; and the barcode reader, which reads the printed bars on product packaging.

bodyText:
What is an Output Device?

An output device is a hardware component that presents the result of processing to the user. After the computer processes input data, the output device converts the processed information into a human-readable form, such as text on a screen, print on paper, or sound from a speaker.

Monitor

The monitor, also called a Visual Display Unit (VDU), is the most common output device. It displays text, images, and video.

Monitor types include CRT, LCD, LED, and OLED displays. CRT stands for Cathode Ray Tube and was used in older, bulky monitors. LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display and uses liquid crystals to form images. LED stands for Light Emitting Diode; an LED monitor is an LCD monitor lit by LEDs. OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diode and produces its own light for each pixel.

Monitor quality is described by resolution, refresh rate, and screen size. Resolution is the number of pixels shown on the screen, written as width by height. Refresh rate is measured in hertz (Hz) and shows how many times per second the image is redrawn. Common monitor connections are VGA, HDMI, and DisplayPort.

Printer

A printer produces a hard copy of output on paper. Printers are classified as impact printers or non-impact printers.

Impact printers strike an inked ribbon against the paper to print characters, like a typewriter. The dot matrix printer is the main impact printer; it prints with a matrix of small pins. Non-impact printers do not strike the paper. Inkjet printers spray tiny drops of ink onto the paper, and laser printers use a laser beam and toner powder to print.

Printer speed is measured in PPM, or pages per minute, and print quality is measured in DPI, or dots per inch. Laser printers are generally faster and give sharper text than inkjet printers, while inkjet printers are commonly used for low-cost colour printing at home.

Speaker

A speaker is an output device that produces sound. The computer sends digital audio signals through a sound card, which converts them into sound waves that the speaker plays. Speakers are used for music, videos, voice calls, and system alerts. Headphones and earphones perform the same function for a single listener.

Other Output Devices

Other output devices include the projector, which displays the computer screen on a large surface; the plotter, which draws large, precise diagrams and engineering drawings; and the plotter and braille printer, which produce output that can be read by touch.
keyPoints: An output device presents processed results in human-readable form, such as screen, print, or sound.

bodyText:
What is a Storage Device?

A storage device is hardware used to store data and programs so that they can be used later. Primary storage, such as RAM, is fast but temporary and loses its contents when the power is switched off. Secondary storage is non-volatile: it keeps data even when the power is off. The devices in this subtopic are all secondary storage devices.

Hard Disk Drive (HDD)

An HDD is a magnetic storage device. It stores data on spinning metal disks called platters, which are coated with a magnetic material. A read-write head moves over the platters to read and write data. Because it has moving parts, an HDD is slower and more easily damaged by shocks than a solid-state drive, but it usually offers a large capacity at a low cost per gigabyte.

The first hard disk drive was the IBM 305 RAMAC, introduced in 1956. Its storage capacity was very small by modern standards, but it was the beginning of disk storage for computers.

Solid State Drive (SSD)

An SSD stores data on NAND flash memory chips and has no moving parts. Because there are no spinning disks or moving heads, an SSD is faster, quieter, and more resistant to shocks than an HDD. SSDs are now commonly used as the main drive in laptops and desktop computers, especially where speed matters, such as starting the operating system and loading programs.

USB Flash Drive

A USB flash drive, also called a pen drive or thumb drive, is a small, portable storage device that uses flash memory. It connects to a computer through a USB port. USB stands for Universal Serial Bus. USB flash drives are used to transfer files between computers and to carry documents, because they are small, light, and easy to use.

Optical Discs: CD and DVD

Optical discs store data using light. A laser reads tiny pits and lands on the surface of the disc. A CD, or Compact Disc, was originally developed for audio and later used for computer data; a standard CD holds about 700 MB. A DVD, or Digital Versatile Disc, holds much more than a CD: a single-layer DVD holds 4.7 GB. A Blu-ray disc, the later optical format, holds 25 GB on a single layer.

Optical discs are read-only in their ROM form, such as CD-ROM and DVD-ROM, while recordable forms such as CD-R and DVD-R can be written once, and rewritable forms such as CD-RW and DVD-RW can be written many times.
keyPoints: Secondary storage is non-volatile: it keeps data even when the power is switched off.

bodyText:
What is the CPU?

The CPU, or Central Processing Unit, is the main processing unit of a computer. It is often called the brain of the computer because it carries out instructions, performs calculations, and controls the other parts of the system. The CPU works in a repeated cycle of three steps: fetch an instruction from memory, decode it to understand what it asks for, and execute it.

The CPU has three main parts: the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), the Control Unit (CU), and the registers. Together with the memory unit, these parts follow the stored-program design described by the von Neumann architecture, in which both instructions and data are held in memory.

Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)

The ALU is the part of the CPU that performs calculations and logical operations. Arithmetic operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Logic operations include comparisons, such as checking whether one value is greater than another, and logical operations such as AND, OR, and NOT. The result of an ALU operation is usually held in the accumulator register before it is stored in memory.

Control Unit (CU)

The CU directs and coordinates all the operations of the computer. It fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and sends control signals to the ALU, the registers, and the input and output devices so that each instruction is carried out in the correct order. The CU does not itself perform calculations or process data; its job is control and coordination. The clock of the CPU sets the pace at which the CU issues these signals, and clock speed is measured in hertz, commonly gigahertz (GHz) in modern processors.

Registers

Registers are very small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU itself. They hold data, instructions, and addresses that the CPU is currently working with. Because they are inside the CPU, registers are the fastest form of memory in a computer, faster than cache memory and RAM, but they hold only a very small amount of data.

The most important registers are the Program Counter (PC), which holds the address of the next instruction to be executed; the Instruction Register (IR), which holds the instruction currently being executed; the Memory Address Register (MAR), which holds the address of the memory location being accessed; the Memory Data Register (MDR), also called the Memory Buffer Register, which holds the data being transferred to or from memory; and the Accumulator, which holds intermediate results of ALU operations. General-purpose registers hold temporary data during processing.
keyPoints: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit and is called the brain of the computer.
The CPU cycle has three steps: fetch, decode, and execute.
The three main parts of the CPU are the ALU, the CU, and the registers.

The ALU also performs logic operations such as AND, OR, NOT, and comparisons.
CU stands for Control Unit.
